References

‘Illegal worker’ refers to an individual who is disqualified from carrying out the work in question by reason of their immigration status. This includes an individual who has not been granted leave to enter or remain in the UK, or whose leave to enter or remain in the UK, either:

is invalid

has ceased to have effect (meaning it no longer applies) whether by reason of curtailment, revocation, cancellation, passage of time or otherwise

is subject to a condition preventing them from accepting the employment, such as not being permitted to work, restrictions on the type of work that can be conducted or limits on the number of hours that can be worked

For the purposes of the Scheme and civil penalty liability, the individual must be aged 16 or over.

A civil penalty is the sanction applied to employers in most routine cases involving illegal workers. An employer will not have a statutory excuse against liability for a civil penalty if they know, or have reasonable cause to believe, that they are employing an individual who is disqualified from working by reason of their immigration status. In these circumstances, the employer may also commit a criminal offence under section 21 of the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006 (IANA 2006). Where appropriate, prosecution may be considered.

‘Breach’ or ‘breaches’ of the Right to Work Scheme occurs where a person employs or engages an illegal worker in circumstances in which they are liable for a civil penalty under section 15 of the IANA 2006.

A breach of the scheme should not be confused with an individual working in breach of the conditions of their immigration permission, for example by carrying out work they are not permitted to do or working more hours than permitted. A failure to comply with conditions of permission may require consideration of cancellation action in respect of the individual’s immigration permission. Separate guidance applies to cancellation action. See Cancellation and Curtailment of permission.

‘Employer’ means a person who employs an individual either:

under a contract of employment (a contract of service or apprenticeship)

under a worker’s contract

as an individual sub-contractor

when operating as an online matching service providing the details of an individual who is a service provider to potential clients or customers

In the context of this guidance, the definition of ‘employer’ is in relation to the Right to Work Scheme only.

References to ‘employment’ or ‘employ’ include the types of working arrangements described and references to a ‘contract’ include a contract that is express or implied, and whether oral or in writing.

Where specified elsewhere in this guidance, references to an employer may include any other person who is liable for a civil penalty under the relevant legislation.

‘Individual sub-contractor’ means an individual who has entered into a contract with a person to provide work or services, in circumstances where that other person has entered into a contract with a third party to provide, or arrange for the provision of, the work or services but the individual has not.

‘Online matching service’ means a person who, in the course of a business:

keeps a register of service providers for the purpose of matching them with potential clients or customers

provides an online service by which potential clients or customers can submit enquiries for the purpose of being matched with suitable service providers

charges a fee or commission in return for making such matches

All 3 elements must be met for a business to fall within the definition of an online matching service for the purposes of the scheme.

See ‘Additional questions for online matching services’ for guidance on gathering information about this working arrangement.

‘Person’ means a company, organisation, business, or other entity, and does not refer to an individual worker unless expressly stated.

‘Right to work’ means allowed to be employed by virtue of qualifying immigration status.

‘Right to work checks’ refer to prescribed manual document checks, prescribed Home Office online right to work checks and prescribed use of a Right to Work Digital Verification Service Provider for these checks.

‘Statutory excuse’ refers to both:

an employer’s defence against liability for payment of a civil penalty, which is established where the employer carries out prescribed right to work checks before the worker commences employment, and where applicable, retains that excuse by carrying out required follow-up checks for workers with a time-limited right to work (as shown by an expiry date)

a person’s defence against extended liability for payment of a civil penalty, which is established where that person has complied with prescribed requirements in relation to the relevant contractual arrangements

‘Substitution’ refers to where a worker is permitted to substitute their work or services to another individual. This includes through a clause or provision in a contract that allows a worker to be replaced by another individual to perform the same work or services.

‘Worker’ or ‘individual’ means an individual who is engaged to carry out work or provide services under a contract of employment (employee), a worker’s contract, as an individual sub-contractor, or through an online matching service, as defined for the purposes of the Right to Work Scheme.

In the context of this guidance, the definition of worker is broader than the definition in s.230(3)(b) of the Employment Rights Act 1996.

Potential extended liability

Where potential extended liability is identified during a visit, you must issue a NOPL to each potentially liable employer or person present at the premises. This may require more than 1 NOPL to be issued.

You are not required to determine whether the prescribed contractual requirements have been met or whether the evidence establishes a statutory excuse under the extended liability provisions. You must record and retain all relevant evidence and provide it to CPCT so that it can assess the contractual arrangements and determine liability.

Where another potentially liable person or business is not present, or their commercial or business premises have not been visited, the absence of a NOPL does not prevent the case from being referred to CPCT for consideration.

Any relevant documents provided should be copied and attached to the Pronto record or sent to the CPCT Referrals inbox quoting the enforcement visit reference number.

Completing and issuing the NOPL

The NOPL must include:

the name and role or job title of the individual to whom it is issued

the date it is issued

the relevant enforcement visit reference

the employer or business name and registered address

the business type

VAT and company number, where applicable

the names of any directors or owners

the date and address at which the illegal working was encountered

the names and dates of birth of the relevant illegal workers

the reason for referral for each worker

You must complete 1 NOPL and as many additional worker supplements (AWS) as required to record all relevant illegal workers.

Where a commercial or business premises is visited, the NOPL must be issued at the time of the visit. You must issue the notice even where further enquiries are required. A photograph of the completed NOPL must be uploaded to Pronto.

Where a potential breach of the Scheme is identified away from the employer’s commercial or business premises, for example where a delivery rider is encountered while making a delivery, there is no requirement to subsequently serve a NOPL on the employer by post. Please note that the absence of a NOPL does not prevent referral to CPCT.

Where the commercial or business premises of a potentially liable employer or person are visited, you must issue a NOPL.

Criminal action

This section explains what you must do when you suspect that a criminal offence has been committed during an illegal working operation.

Suspected criminal offences

If, during exploratory questioning or an administrative interview, you develop reasonable grounds to suspect that a criminal offence may have been committed you must stop questioning about the suspected offence and refer the matter to the appropriate Criminal and Financial Investigations (CFI) team or CFI duty manager as soon as possible.

This may include suspected offences relating to:

employing an illegal worker

illegal working

facilitation

modern slavery, human trafficking, forced labour, or related offences

You must record the referral and follow any advice provided by CFI to ensure that any subsequent arrest, interview, or seizure of evidence is conducted in accordance with the relevant legislation and guidance.

Where CFI advises that an individual should be arrested, you must caution the individual and explain the reason for their arrest. See: Arrest and restraint.

For further information on questioning and interviews, see: Enforcement interviews.

Civil penalty and criminal action

A potential civil penalty and a suspected criminal offence may arise from the same circumstances.

Where you suspect that an employer may be liable for a civil penalty, but do not suspect that the employer has committed a criminal offence, you may continue to gather the information necessary for evidencing a breach of the scheme.

Where you suspect that an employer has also committed a criminal offence, you must stop questioning about the suspected offence and seek advice from CFI.

A worker may commit the offence of illegal working whether or not civil or criminal action is taken against an employer. Where criminal action against the worker may be appropriate, refer the matter to CFI.

CFI will determine whether criminal action is appropriate in accordance with the relevant guidance and circumstances of the case. See also:

Arrest and restraint

Enforcement interviews

Dealing with potential criminality

Identifying people at risk

Supporting employers

This section explains how to respond where an employer asks you for advice about preventing illegal working or reports suspected illegal working.

You must take care when advising employers and ensure that any advice is consistent with published Home Office guidance. You must not advise an employer on individual employment decisions or provide assurances about whether or not civil penalty or criminal action will be taken in cases involving illegal working.

Cooperation by an employer does not prevent civil penalty or criminal action. Relevant mitigating factors will be considered as part of any subsequent civil penalty or criminal investigation process.

General advice about preventing illegal working

Employers seeking general advice about preventing illegal working or help conducting a right to work check should be directed to the relevant employer support services and GOV.UK guidance:

The Home Office Employer Enquiry helpline on 0300 790 6268

Penalties for employing illegal workers which provides access to guidance on preventing illegal working
